tldr: We developed 3D-printed origami wheels that simultaneously morph their width, diameter, and fin orientation, enabling a single compact amphibious robot to efficiently traverse everything from firm soil and wet mud to sand and water.
hero_caption: MOSS traversing diverse wetland-like environments including sand, mud, and water. By switching its wheel geometry to match the terrain, it transitions seamlessly from land to water.
overview:
Wetlands and swamps are vital for ecological monitoring, but they mix firm ground, dry sand, waterlogged mud, and open water in complex ways. Conventional fixed-geometry wheels cannot balance the trade-off between reducing rolling resistance on firm ground and preventing sinkage and slip on soft ground.

To solve this, the authors developed MOSS, a compact amphibious robot equipped with morphing origami wheels. A simple crank mechanism pushes or pulls the wheel along its axis, simultaneously changing wheel width, body diameter, and fin orientation. To transmit driving torque while allowing the wheel to morph, they also designed a novel dual telescopic shaft.

The team conducted rigorous locomotion tests across soil, sand, three types of mud with varying water contents, and water. On firm soil and low-water mud, the contracted (narrow, large-diameter) configuration reduced rolling resistance and saved energy. On wet mud, sand, and water, the expanded (wide, small-diameter) configuration distributed contact pressure, cut wheel slip, and reduced the Cost of Transport (CoT) by up to 29%. With smooth in-motion morphing and successful outdoor wetland trials, the robot clearly demonstrates the value of terrain-adaptive mobility.
contributions: A design and manufacturing method for 3D-printed morphing origami wheels, incorporating mudskipper-inspired fins and optimized for thick-panel folding
A coaxial telescopic shaft mechanism that enables axial wheel morphing while transmitting driving torque and resisting lateral bending loads
Systematic locomotion experiments across soil, sand, mud with varying water content, and water, proving that terrain properties clearly flip which wheel configuration is advantageous
Real-world demonstrations of dynamic in-motion morphing (~1.95 s) and autonomous traversal across continuous soil–mud–water composite terrains

sections.heading: How do you traverse harsh wetlands? The idea of morphing wheels
sections.summary: Wetlands mix firm ground, mud, and water, making traversal difficult for mobile robots with fixed-geometry wheels. This work presents MOSS, a compact amphibious robot with origami-inspired wheels that change width, diameter, and fin orientation to tackle this challenge.
sections.details:
Wetlands and swamps support rich biodiversity and play a crucial role in carbon sequestration and water purification. However, they are tough for humans to enter regularly, and water levels and soil conditions shift drastically with the seasons. Long-term automated robot monitoring is sorely needed.

The biggest hurdle is extreme terrain diversity. Slim wheels with low rolling resistance are great for smooth travel on firm ground, but on soft mud or loose sand, a narrow contact patch causes the wheels to sink and slip severely. In short, different terrains demand completely opposite wheel characteristics.

Transformable and origami-structured wheels have been explored before. Yet integrating axial expansion, thrust-generating fins, and reliable driving torque transmission into a compact robot footprint has remained very difficult. Comprehensive mobility evaluations across varying mud water contents and terrestrial-aquatic transitions have also been lacking. MOSS was developed to tackle all of these challenges at once.

sections.heading: 3D-printed origami wheels with mudskipper-inspired fins
sections.summary: Based on Mitani's origami sphere, the pattern was adapted for 3D-printing with thick panels. A single push-pull action roughly doubles wheel width, reduces diameter, and passively reorients surface fins to boost traction in mud and water.
sections.details:
### II-A Origami Wheel Structure and Manufacturing
The wheel is based on the "rotational-sweep origami sphere" proposed by Mitani. Unlike paper, 3D printing materials have thickness, so they cannot be folded directly. The team varied panel thickness across three levels—0.1 mm, 0.2 mm, and 0.7 mm—integrating thin regions as hinges and thick regions as load-bearing facets in a single print.

Because PLA resin fatigues easily under cyclic bending, compliance cutouts were placed at key creases and reinforced with flexible fabric tape. Overlapping panels like an isopod's carapace provide both circumferential strength and structural flexibility. By actuating a central link, the wheel transitions from a contracted configuration (27 mm wide, 95 mm diameter) to an expanded configuration (53 mm wide, 73 mm diameter), roughly doubling its width.

### II-B Integrated Fins and Coupled Morphing
Fins inspired by the pectoral fins of mudskippers—animals that move agilely across tidal flats—are directly integrated onto the wheel surface. As the wheel morphs, the tilted panels rotate, passively changing the fin angle $\alpha$. In the contracted state, the fins sit nearly parallel to the ground ($\alpha \approx 85^{\circ}$). When expanded, the angle sharpens, allowing the fins to paddle through soft mud and sand to generate forward thrust.

### II-C Crank Drive and Shape Retention
Wheel morphing is driven by a central servo motor and a crank mechanism. While the inner hub remains axially fixed to the chassis, links push and pull the outer hub. The servo's position-holding torque maintains the wheel's shape, eliminating the need for a dedicated mechanical locking mechanism and keeping the design simple.

(b) Dimension comparison between expanded and contracted configurations, roughly doubling the width. (c) Morphing and drive mechanisms using a crank linkage and dual telescopic shaft.

sections.heading: A telescopic shaft balancing drive torque and axial morphing, plus robot integration
sections.summary: To decouple axial morphing from rotational driving, the team designed a telescopic shaft combining brass tubing and a carbon rod. Efficient packaging of motors and electronics inside a compact body yields a lightweight 560 g robot.
sections.details:
### III-A Balancing Axial Morphing and Torque Transmission
Simultaneously transmitting rotational torque while expanding or contracting a wheel axially is mechanically tricky. Coil springs used in prior work lack lateral stiffness and bend under load, while tendon-driven setups add complexity. The authors resolved this with a telescopic shaft that cleanly separates axial sliding from rotation.

An outer shaft rotates to deliver driving torque, while a chassis-mounted servo slides an inner 2 mm carbon rod axially to morph the wheel. A brass intermediate sleeve (3 mm outer diameter, 2 mm inner diameter) guides the assembly. Cantilever beam mechanics showed that under a 2.75 N lateral load at full expansion, an unguided carbon rod would deflect by 9.7 to 14.6 mm. The brass tube, with roughly four times the second moment of area, provides ample bending stiffness.

### III-B Robot Platform and Electronics
The entire robot weighs just 560 g, and each wheel weighs only about 40 g. The left and right wheels are driven independently by Dynamixel servos through 6:1 herringbone gear sets. Offsetting the gears provides clean routing clearance for the telescopic shaft. A 45-degree angled splash guard at the bow shields onboard electronics from mud and water spray.

A Raspberry Pi Compute Module 4 serves as the onboard computer, running ROS 2 Humble at 50 Hz to handle actuator control and sensor logging. Power is supplied by a 3-cell (850 mAh) LiPo battery.

### III-C Kinematic Model and Odometry
The robot follows a standard differential-drive kinematic model. Instead of relying on a purely geometric radius, the model uses a calibrated effective rolling radius that accounts for fin contact and terrain engagement. Calibrated on rigid ground, the effective radius is $R_{\mathrm{ref,C}} = 42.9~\mathrm{mm}$ in the contracted state and $R_{\mathrm{ref,E}} = 49.0~\mathrm{mm}$ in the expanded state. These values allow accurate calculation of vehicle speed and odometry from encoder data.

captions.F3: Overall design of the MOSS robot. (a) Placement of the morphing crank servo and independent drive motors. (b, c) Chassis dimensions. Wheel tread changes from 243 mm contracted to 260 mm expanded. An angled bow guard prevents mud and water ingress.

sections.heading: Soil, mud, sand, and water: Controlled test environments and evaluation metrics
sections.summary: Locomotion tests were conducted across soil, sand, three mud consistencies, and water inside an acrylic testbed. Motion capture and high-speed imaging objectively evaluated slip ratio, hub sinkage, and Cost of Transport (CoT).
sections.details:
### IV-A Test Environments and Payload Conditions
Experiments were conducted in a $100\times 50\times 10~\mathrm{cm}$ acrylic testbed. A 3 cm thick substrate layer was prepared using dry soil (4.7 kg), sand, and three mud mixtures with varying water-to-soil weight ratios: Mud0.5 (0.5x water), Mud1.0 (1.0x water), and very soft Mud2.0 (2.0x water). Each mud mixture was stirred for 10 minutes and rested for 10 minutes, with soil moisture sensors verifying consistency across trials.

To study the effect of payload, tests evaluated three loading conditions: 0 g, 100 g, and 200 g weights placed near the wheel axis. Water trials evaluated 0 g and 100 g due to buoyancy constraints.

### IV-B Evaluation Metrics: Slip, Sinkage, and Cost of Transport
Vehicle pose was tracked using a Vicon motion capture system, while hub sinkage ratio ($S_{\mathrm{hub}}$) was measured from lateral camera footage. Slip ratio was defined as $i = (v_{\mathrm{ref}} - v_{\mathrm{real}}) / v_{\mathrm{ref}}$, where $v_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the no-slip reference speed from encoders and $v_{\mathrm{real}}$ is the actual ground speed.

Energy efficiency was quantified using the dimensionless Cost of Transport, $\mathrm{CoT} = E_{\mathrm{move}} / (m g d)$, where $E_{\mathrm{move}}$ is the integrated electrical energy consumed during motion, $m$ is total mass, and $d$ is travel distance. This metric isolates locomotion efficiency in a given wheel configuration without factoring in morphing actuation energy.

### IV-C Continuous Transitions and In-Motion Morphing
To test multi-terrain capabilities, a composite course combining soil, mud (Mud2.0), and open water in sequence was built to measure transition success rates. In-motion morphing tests also evaluated wheel configuration switching while driving, confirming that wheel rotation relieves ground friction for smoother actuation than morphing while stationary.

sections.heading: The optimal wheel shape flips with terrain: Experimental results and field trials
sections.summary: Experiments revealed that contracted wheels are more energy-efficient on firm soil and dense mud, whereas expanded wheels cut slip and sinkage on wet mud, sand, and water. Outdoor wetland trials also verified smooth land-to-water traversal.
sections.details:
### V-A Morphing Reliability and Energy Consumption
Crank-actuated configuration switching completed in an average of $1.95 \pm 0.11~\mathrm{s}$. The energy consumed was 2.26 J when contracting and 1.48 J when expanding. While morphing from a standstill must overcome static ground friction, morphing while rolling significantly reduced resistance, achieving reliable shape transitions with a 100% success rate.

### V-B A Clear Terrain-Dependent Trade-Off
Locomotion experiments highlighted an intriguing trade-off: neither configuration is universally superior.
- **Dramatic gains in sand**: In the contracted state, slip reached ~45% and sinkage hit 33.3%. Expanding the wheels dropped slip by 13 percentage points to ~32% and limited sinkage to 24.7%. Speed increased by ~32%, and CoT improved by about 26% (falling from 2.9 to 2.1).
- **High-moisture mud (Mud2.0)**: Expanding the wheels reduced slip from 14.9% to 12.9% and also improved CoT.
- **Water surface propulsion**: In the expanded state, the wider profile and upright fins acted like paddle wheels, boosting travel speed by ~47% and slashing CoT by about 29%.
- **Firm soil and dense mud (Mud0.5, Mud1.0)**: Here, the trend completely reversed. The contracted state yielded lower slip (8.4% vs. 11.6% on soil) and lower rolling resistance, leading to a better CoT. On firm ground, slim wheels without excessive contact area or fin interference are clearly superior.

### V-C Payload Effects and Robot Benchmarking
Adding payload increased normal force, which boosted soil shear strength in sand and reduced slip. When benchmarked against other amphibious robots and biological organisms (amphibians), MOSS demonstrated well-balanced, high energy efficiency across both soft terrain and water.

### V-D Composite Transitions and Outdoor Field Trials
In laboratory traverse trials across continuous soil–mud–water paths, MOSS achieved an 80% success rate (8 out of 10 runs). The two failures occurred when the chassis underbody beached against the rigid step transition between mud and water, revealing a ground clearance limitation. In outdoor wetland trials, MOSS equipped with a camera, microphone, and passive floats smoothly navigated from peatland into duckweed-covered water without issue.

(c) Slip ratio and hub sinkage ratio across terrains; sand shows a dramatic slip reduction when expanded. (d) Cost of Transport (CoT) versus average speed. Bottom-right indicates higher speed and efficiency, clearly showing expanded wheels (squares) excel on soft terrain and water, while contracted wheels (circles) excel on firm ground.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: The next steps for terrain-adaptive mobility
sections.summary: MOSS demonstrated that combining morphing origami wheels with a telescopic shaft enables high-efficiency traversal across mud, sand, and water. Future work will focus on high-friction tread materials, self-locking mechanisms, and autonomous terrain perception.
sections.details:
This study presented MOSS, an origami-inspired morphing amphibious robot, and experimentally validated its mechanical and energetic benefits across complex wetland environments.

The coupled design that morphs width, diameter, and fin angle with a single actuator—supported by a dual telescopic shaft—achieves an impressive balance of lightness, compactness, and structural strength. Most importantly, the paper provides clear, quantitative evidence that no single wheel shape is optimal for every surface; active terrain adaptation is key to true high-efficiency locomotion.

The authors outline several exciting avenues for future improvement:
- **Self-locking mechanisms**: Currently, the morphing servo draws continuous holding power to maintain its shape. Incorporating a bistable or over-center linkage would allow passive locking and eliminate standby power draw.
- **Improved friction materials**: Adding high-friction rubber to the wheel treads could further boost traction.
- **Autonomous terrain sensing**: Equipping the robot with onboard sensors to estimate terrain softness and moisture in real time will enable fully autonomous, seamless wheel adaptation on the fly.

With these advancements, MOSS-like platforms could become a standard tool for demanding field missions, from post-flood disaster inspection to long-term ecological monitoring.

takeaways: Origami engineering combined with 3D-printed panel thickness tuning allows monolithic fabrication of multifunctional wheels that morph width, diameter, and fin orientation without complex multi-link assemblies.
A coaxial telescopic shaft that decouples sliding morphing from rotational torque transmission enables a lightweight (40 g per wheel) and compact morphing mechanism.

Morphological adaptation—contracting to minimize rolling resistance on firm ground, expanding to maximize contact area and paddle effect on soft ground and water—reduces Cost of Transport by up to 29%.
Morphing while rolling dramatically relieves ground friction compared to stationary morphing, enabling smoother configuration changes with lower actuation effort.
limitations: The robot relies on active servo position holding to maintain its wheel configuration, constantly drawing electrical power just to stay in shape (lack of a self-locking mechanism).
The chassis has limited underbody ground clearance (~33 mm), creating a risk of high-centering or getting beached on rigid obstacles, such as the lip between the mud and water tank.
Because wheel width, diameter, and fin angle are geometrically coupled, the experimental setup could not isolate the individual contribution of each morphological factor to locomotion gains.
